title: Rivals Themistocles and Aristides Unite at Salamis
text:
Themistocles and Aristides had been the bitterest rivals in Athenian politics. In 482 BC Themistocles' faction had Aristides ostracized, sent into exile for ten years. But when Xerxes invaded Greece in 480, Athens recalled its exiles.

In September the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, and the allied commanders were quarreling over whether to retreat to the Isthmus. Themistocles wanted to fight in the narrow strait. That night the Persian fleet moved to block both ends of the channel.

Herodotus says Aristides crossed from Aegina, slipped past the enemy ships, and called Themistocles out of the council. He told him that they should always be rivals, but now especially, over which of them could do more good for their country. Then he reported that the Greeks were surrounded. Themistocles was delighted: the Persians had done exactly what he had tricked them into doing. He asked Aristides to tell the other commanders himself, since they would not believe Themistocles.

Plutarch adds that Aristides proposed they lay aside their "vain and childish contention" and compete only in saving Greece, and that when a Corinthian sneered that Aristides was silent in council, he replied that he would not be silent if Themistocles were not giving the best advice. In the battle that followed, the Greeks won, and Aristides led a force that cleared the Persians off the islet of Psyttaleia in the strait.
lesson: Rivals can still be teammates. When the stakes are shared, compete only over who contributes more, and back a good idea even when it comes from your opponent.
source: Herodotus, Histories 8.79 to 8.82 and 8.95; Plutarch, Life of Aristides 8 to 9
